197.title: Sins first (Mark 2:1–12)
197.hook: the paralyzed man hears his sins forgiven before he hears walk
197.tomorrow: the sabbath was made for man
197.howItsDone: Catholics receive forgiveness in the sacrament of reconciliation, or confession, where a priest speaks the words of absolution; this gospel is read at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, if thou wilt: a leper, and a hand that reached out. Your line was he touched him. Who did you reach? Today, four friends and a hole in a roof. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Jesus is back in Capernaum, and word gets around. The house is so packed there's no room even at the door. Then four men arrive carrying their friend on a mat. He can't walk. They can't get in. So they do what good friends do when the front door fails. They climb up on the flat roof, dig a hole straight through it, and lower him down on ropes, right in front of Jesus, while dust and bits of roof fall on everybody's heads. Everyone knows what the man needs. And Jesus says something nobody expects. Today: sins first.
screen: `A PACKED HOUSE.` → `FOUR FRIENDS ON THE ROOF.` → `A HOLE, AND A MAT ON ROPES.`

segments.voice: First, whose faith. Mark says Jesus saw their faith, the friends' faith. The man on the mat hasn't said a word. Somebody else's trust carried him in. Second, the surprise. Jesus looks at the man and says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Not get up. Not be healed. Forgiven. The friends must have looked at each other. That's not what we came for. Third, the scribes. Some teachers of the law are sitting there, and they think it silently: "Why doth this man speak thus? he blasphemeth. Who can forgive sins, but God only?" In one way, they've understood exactly. Only God can forgive sins against God. That's the point Mark wants you to feel. Then Jesus asks: which is easier, to say your sins are forgiven, or to say get up and walk? Anyone can say the first; nobody can check it. So, to show that the Son of man has power on earth to forgive sins, he says to the man: arise, take up thy bed, and go home. And he does, in front of everyone. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. Jesus never says the man's sin caused his paralysis. The gospels push back against that idea elsewhere. The story is about order: Jesus goes for the deeper healing first, the one nobody could see. Catholics hear in this story the root of confession. They believe Christ gave his apostles a share in this power to forgive, and that it continues in the sacrament of reconciliation today.
screen: `THEY CARRIED HIM ON THEIR FAITH.` · `FORGIVEN, NOT WALK.` · `WHO CAN FORGIVE SINS BUT GOD?` · `THE DEEPER HEALING FIRST.` · then, large: `SON, THY SINS ARE FORGIVEN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for what you most need. Settle, and breathe. Start with what you think you need today: a fix, an answer, more time. Name it. Now go one layer down. What's underneath that? Maybe it's to be forgiven, or to forgive. Maybe it's rest, or to stop being afraid. Let the deeper thing come up. If you pray, ask God for that one. If you don't, just name it honestly to yourself. The bell holds the time.
Sins first. The paralyzed man hears forgiven before he hears walk: Jesus heals the deeper wound before the visible one. Today's word.
Your line: the deeper healing first. Today, when you're helping someone, or yourself, ask once what's underneath the problem everybody can see. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

198.title: The sabbath was made for man (Mark 2:13–28)
198.hook: he eats with sinners and says rest serves people, not the reverse
198.howItsDone: Catholics keep Sunday as the Lord's Day by attending Mass and resting from unnecessary work, and the Church teaches that Sunday rest is meant for family, prayer and care for others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sins first: a man through a roof, forgiven before he walked. Your line was the deeper healing first. What did you find underneath? Day one hundred ninety-eight.

Have you ever taken a day off and spent it feeling guilty? Checking email from the couch. Doing chores so the day counts for something. Telling people, I'm resting, but in a tone that sounds like an apology. A lot of us treat rest like a reward we haven't quite earned. In today's reading, Jesus gets into two arguments. One is about who he eats dinner with. The other is about a day of rest, and what it's for. And he settles it with one sentence. Today's word: sabbath.
screen: `A DAY OFF, FULL OF GUILT.` → `TWO ARGUMENTS.` → `ONE SENTENCE SETTLES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the dinner. Jesus walks past a tax collector named Levi, sitting at his booth, and says follow me, and Levi does. Tax collectors worked for the occupiers and were widely seen as traitors and cheats. Then Jesus eats at Levi's house with a crowd of tax collectors and sinners, and people object. He answers in the Douay-Rheims: "They that are well have no need of a physician, but they that are sick." Second, the word. Sabbath is the Hebrew shabbat, from a root meaning to stop, to cease. In Genesis, God rests on the seventh day, and the commandments tell Israel to keep it holy, and to let everyone rest: children, servants, foreigners, even the animals. It's one of the great gifts of Judaism to the world. Third, the argument. On a sabbath, Jesus's disciples pluck heads of grain as they walk through a field. Some Pharisees object that this is work. Jewish teachers debated carefully what counted as work; this was a real question, asked seriously. Jesus answers with a story about David, who ate the holy bread when his men were hungry. And then the sentence: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift for people, not a burden laid on them. Jewish teachers said something very close: a later rabbinic teaching puts it as the sabbath is given to you, not you to the sabbath. Fourth, what Catholics do with it. Christians moved their holy day to Sunday, the day of the resurrection, and Catholics keep it as the Lord's Day: Mass, and rest from needless work.
screen: `LEVI AND A TABLE OF SINNERS.` · `SHABBAT: TO STOP.` · `GRAIN PLUCKED ON THE SABBATH.` · `REST IS A GIFT, NOT A BURDEN.` · then, large: `THE SABBATH WAS MADE FOR MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a real rest, starting now. Settle, and breathe. For these two minutes, you're not improving yourself or getting anything done. You're stopping, which is what sabbath means. If a to-do list shows up in your head, let it go past. Let your shoulders drop, and your jaw. If you pray, you can receive this rest as a gift from God. If you don't, just receive it. The bell holds the time.
Sabbath. From the Hebrew shabbat, to stop: the day of rest, which Jesus says was made for people. Today's word.
Your line: rest is for you. Today, take one real rest, even fifteen minutes, with no guilt and no phone, and don't apologize for it. Day one hundred ninety-eight.

199.title: The twelve (Mark 3:1–19)
199.hook: a withered hand healed, then he names twelve to be with him
199.howItsDone: Catholics keep feast days for each of the apostles through the year, and profess in the Creed that the Church is apostolic, led by bishops understood as the apostles' successors.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sabbath, made for people. Your line was rest is for you. Did you take a real rest, without apologizing? Today, one more sabbath, and then a list of names. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

Think of any team you've been picked for. A class project, a work crew, a band, a game in the park. You probably assume you were picked for what you could do. Your speed, your skills, your ideas. In today's reading Jesus climbs a hill, calls the people he wants, and chooses twelve. Mark lists them by name. And before he says anything about what they'll do, he says why he chose them, and it's not what you'd expect. Today's word is what they were called: apostle.
screen: `PICKED FOR A TEAM.` → `TWELVE CALLED UP A HILL.` → `CHOSEN FOR WHAT?`

segments.voice: First, a hand. It starts on another sabbath, in a synagogue, with a man whose hand is withered. People watch to see what Jesus will do. He asks them, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to destroy?" Nobody answers. Mark says Jesus looked round at them with anger, grieved at the hardness of their hearts. Then he says to the man: stretch forth thy hand. And it's restored. Second, the hill. After this, Jesus goes up a mountain and calls those he wants, and they come. And Mark says: "And he made that twelve should be with him, and that he might send them to preach." Twelve is no accident. Israel had twelve tribes; Jesus is gathering a people. Third, the order. Read it again. First, to be with him. Then, to be sent. Before any preaching or healing, the job is to be with him: walk the roads, eat at the same fire, watch him pray at dawn. Fourth, the names. Simon, whom he names Peter. James and John, whom he nicknames sons of thunder. Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James son of Alphaeus, Thaddeus, Simon the Cananean, and Judas Iscariot, who, Mark tells us right away, would betray him. Fishermen, a tax collector, and a hothead or two. Apostle is Greek, apostolos, one who is sent. Catholics believe the bishops today are the apostles' successors, a line that runs, they say, all the way back to that hill.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: your twelve. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people you really walk through life with, the ones you'd call at two in the morning, the ones who've watched you at your worst. Let their names come one at a time. You may not get to twelve. That's fine. If you can, write them down. If you pray, you can hold each name before God for a moment. If you don't, just be grateful, one name at a time. The bell holds the time.
Apostle. From the Greek apostolos, one who is sent. But in Mark, the twelve are called first to be with him. Today's word.
Your line: first, to be with him. Today, with someone you love, don't try to do anything for them for ten minutes. Just be with them. Day one hundred ninety-nine.

200.title: Who is my mother (Mark 3:20–35)
200.hook: his relatives come; he says whoever does God's will is his family; Catholics read brethren as kin, as Aramaic allows
200.howItsDone: Catholics honor Mary as the first and most faithful disciple, and call one another brothers and sisters in Christ; the Church teaches Mary's perpetual virginity and reads the Lord's brethren as his relatives.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve, the first apostles. Your line was first, to be with him. Who did you simply spend time with? Today is day two hundred. Two hundred days of showing up. Day two hundred.

Every family has had this moment. Someone starts doing something the rest of the family doesn't understand. Quits the job. Joins something. Moves away. And the relatives start talking. Is he all right? Has she lost it? Somebody should go and bring him home. That's where Jesus is today. The crowds are so thick he can't even eat. Mark says his own people hear about it and set out to take charge of him, because they're saying he's out of his mind. And then his mother and brothers arrive, and stand outside, and send someone in to call him. Today: who is my mother.
screen: `THE FAMILY STARTS TALKING.` → `HE'S OUT OF HIS MIND.` → `HIS MOTHER AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Mark tells this as a sandwich: family, then an argument, then family again. First, the middle. Scribes come down from Jerusalem and say Jesus drives out demons by the power of the devil. He answers with a picture: a house divided against itself cannot stand. Why would Satan fight Satan? Second, the doorway. Someone tells him: your mother and your brethren are outside, looking for you. And he says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who is my mother and my brethren?" He looks around at the people sitting in a circle at his feet. "Behold my mother and my brethren. For whosoever shall do the will of God, he is my brother, and my sister, and mother." It can sound cold. It isn't a rejection. It's a widening. The family is open now, to anyone who does God's will. Third, Mary. Catholics notice that no one did God's will more fully than Mary herself, who said yes to God before Jesus was born. Saint Augustine said she was more blessed for being his disciple than for being his mother. So she isn't pushed out by this saying. She's its best example. Fourth, the brethren. Who are they? Christians read this differently. Catholics believe Mary remained a virgin, and read brethren as relatives, kin, since Hebrew and Aramaic used the word brother for cousins and nephews too; in Genesis, Abraham calls his nephew Lot his brother. Orthodox Christians often say they were Joseph's children from an earlier marriage. Many Protestants read them as younger children of Mary and Joseph. Each reads the same verse carefully, and the text itself doesn't settle it.
screen: `A HOUSE DIVIDED CANNOT STAND.` · `BEHOLD MY MOTHER AND MY BRETHREN.` · `MARY: THE BEST EXAMPLE.` · `BRETHREN: KIN, STEP-KIN, OR SIBLINGS?` · then, large: `WHOSOEVER SHALL DO THE WILL OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a stranger as family. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you'll probably pass today without a second look: a cashier, a bus driver, a new kid at school, the neighbor you've never spoken to. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Now picture them sitting in that circle around Jesus, and hear him say: behold my brother, my sister. If you pray, hold them there for a while. If you don't, simply wish them well as you would your own family. The bell holds the time.
Who is my mother. Jesus's question at the door, and his answer: whoever does the will of God is my brother, my sister, my mother. Today's word.
Your line: family by doing God's will. Today, treat one stranger the way you'd treat family: with patience, a real greeting, a little extra time. Day two hundred.

201.title: The sower again (Mark 4:1–20)
201.hook: now read the parable with the explanation beside it
201.tomorrow: the seed that grows while you sleep
201.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parable of the sower at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and many use it for lectio divina, asking which kind of ground they are right now.

segments.voice: Yesterday, who is my mother: a family widened to everyone who does God's will. Your line was family by doing God's will. Which stranger did you treat as kin? Day two hundred one.

You've heard this story before on the path. Back in the stories camp, we met the sower in Matthew's gospel: a farmer flinging seed, some on the path, some on rock, some in thorns, some on good soil. That time, we heard it as a story. Today we're reading Mark straight through, so we meet it again, in Mark's own words, and this time we're going to do what a good reader does: lay the story side by side with the explanation Jesus gives his friends afterward, and look closely at one kind of ground. Today: the sower again.
screen: `WE'VE MET HIM BEFORE.` → `NOW IN MARK'S WORDS.` → `STORY AND EXPLANATION, SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: First, the setting. The crowd is so big that Jesus gets into a boat and sits on the water, teaching the people on the shore. Then he begins, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hear ye: Behold, the sower went out to sow." Four kinds of ground. Seed on the path is eaten by birds. Seed on rock springs up fast and withers in the sun, with no root. Seed among thorns is choked. Seed on good ground yields thirty, sixty, a hundredfold. And he ends: he that hath ears to hear, let him hear. Second, the explanation. Later, alone with the twelve, Jesus explains it line by line. The seed is the word. The path is the person the word never gets into. The rock is the one who welcomes it with joy but falls away when trouble comes. And good ground is the one who hears, receives, and bears fruit. Third, the thorns. Look at these closely, because they're the ones most of us live among. "And the cares of the world, and the deceitfulness of riches, and the lusts after other things entering in choke the word, and it is made fruitless." Notice: the thorns don't kill the seed on the first day. The seed sprouts. It grows. It's just slowly crowded out by worry, by money, by wanting other things, until nothing comes of it. Nobody decides to stop listening. It gets choked. Fourth, the harvest. A hundredfold would have sounded astonishing to people who farmed that land. The parable ends not in failure but in more than anyone expected.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the thorns in your week. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last few days. What choked the good things? Not a disaster, just the slow crowding. A worry you kept circling. Money on your mind. Wanting something so much it filled the room. Name one thorn. Don't pull it out yet. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can show it to God. If you don't, just notice how much room it takes up. The bell holds the time.
The sower again. The parable of four kinds of ground, read now in Mark, with Jesus's own explanation beside it. Today's word.
Your line: the thorns are the cares. Today, when one worry starts crowding everything else, name it as a thorn, and give the good seed a little room. Day two hundred one.

202.title: The seed that grows while you sleep (Mark 4:21–34)
202.word: The seed that grows while you sl
202.hook: a lamp on its stand, and seed that grows though the sower doesn't know how
202.howItsDone: Catholics hear the parables of the growing seed and the mustard seed at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and often read them as a lesson in patience and trust in God's work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sower again, and the thorns that choke. Your line was the thorns are the cares. Which worry did you name? Today, more seeds, and a parable only Mark tells. Day two hundred two.

If you've ever planted anything, a bean in a paper cup at school, tomatoes on a balcony, you know the temptation. You check it every morning. You want to dig it up just a little to see if anything's happening. You water it too much. And nothing you do makes it go faster. Then one day, there it is, a green thread poking out of the dirt, and you didn't see it happen. It happened at night, or while you were at work, without you. Jesus told a parable about exactly that, and only Mark kept it. Today: the seed that grows while you sleep.
screen: `A BEAN IN A PAPER CUP.` → `CHECKING EVERY MORNING.` → `IT GREW WITHOUT YOU.`

segments.voice: Jesus is still teaching from the boat, and he gives a handful of short sayings and parables. First, the lamp. Nobody lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel basket or under a bed. You put it on the lampstand. What's hidden is meant to come to light. Second, the seed that grows by itself. This one is only in Mark. In the Douay-Rheims: "So is the kingdom of God, as if a man should cast seed into the earth, And should sleep, and rise, night and day, and the seed should spring, and grow up whilst he knoweth not." He sleeps. He gets up. He goes about his days. And the seed grows, and he doesn't know how. "For the earth of itself bringeth forth fruit, first the blade, then the ear, afterwards the full corn in the ear." Of itself: in Greek, automatē, the word English turned into automatic. Third, what it means. The farmer's work is real: he sows, and when it's ripe, he harvests. But the growing isn't his. Christians hear this about the kingdom of God, and about faith in a person's life: it grows in stages, often unseen, and it isn't all up to you. For anyone who worries they're not doing enough, that's a relief. Fourth, the mustard seed. The kingdom is like the smallest of seeds that becomes a plant so large birds can nest in its shade. Small beginnings. Hidden growth. A surprising size. Mark says Jesus taught many parables like these, and explained everything privately to his disciples.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust one thing to grow. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you've planted that you keep digging up to check on. A friendship you're trying to mend. A kid who's finding their way. A habit you've started. A prayer you keep praying. Picture it as a seed in dark soil. You've done your part. Now let it be. If you pray, you can hand it to God to grow. If you don't, just practice not checking on it, for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The seed that grows while you sleep. Mark's parable of the kingdom that grows of itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain. Today's word.

203.title: Peace, be still (Mark 4:35–41)
203.hook: reading the storm again: why are you fearful
203.howItsDone: Catholics hear the calming of the storm at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and many pray 'peace, be still' in times of fear; Pope Francis preached on this passage in an empty St. Peter's Square during the 2020 pandemic.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seed that grows while you sleep. Your line was it grows while you sleep. Did you leave something to grow on its own? Today, the same evening, out on the lake. Day two hundred three.

We've met this storm before, back in the stories. Now we're reading Mark in order, and you can see where it falls: at the end of the same long day of parables. Jesus has been teaching from a boat since morning. Evening comes, and he says, let's cross to the other side. They push off, just as they are. And the Sea of Galilee does what it's known for: a sudden wind drops down from the hills, the waves pour over the sides, and the boat starts filling with water. These are fishermen. They know when a boat is going down. Today's word: peace.
screen: `THE SAME LONG DAY.` → `LET US CROSS OVER.` → `A SUDDEN STORM.`

segments.voice: First, the sleeper. Mark gives a detail no other gospel keeps. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he was in the hinder part of the ship, sleeping upon a pillow; and they awake him, and say to him: Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" A cushion in the stern. Exhausted, after a whole day of teaching. And the disciples don't only ask for help. They ask, don't you care? Plenty of prayers sound like that. Second, the command. He gets up and rebukes the wind and says to the sea: "Peace, be still." In Mark's Greek, be still is literally be muzzled, the same word he used when Jesus silenced a demon in Capernaum. The wind stops, and there's a great calm. Third, the question to them. "Why are you fearful? have you not faith yet?" Not yet. Mark's disciples are slow learners, and he doesn't hide it. Fourth, their question. Now they're more afraid than they were in the storm, and they say to each other: "Who is this (thinkest thou) that both wind and sea obey him?" Here's why that question matters, and why we just spent five weeks in the Psalms. In the Hebrew Bible, only God rules the sea. The psalms say it again and again: God stills the roaring waves, God makes the storm a calm. So when the wind obeys Jesus, the disciples are left staring at a question the psalms seem to answer. Mark doesn't answer it for them yet. He lets it hang there, in a quiet boat, in the dark. This week began with sins forgiven, and it ends with the sea obeying. Who is this?
screen: `ASLEEP ON A CUSHION.` · `PEACE, BE MUZZLED.` · `HAVE YOU NOT FAITH YET?` · `ONLY GOD RULES THE SEA.` · then, large: `WHO IS THIS THAT BOTH WIND AND SEA OBEY HIM?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name the storm and say the words. Settle, and breathe. What's the storm this week? Name it plainly: the bill, the diagnosis, the argument, the fear that wakes you. Picture it as wind and water in a small boat. Now, if you pray, say the words into it, slowly: peace, be still. You can say them as a prayer to Christ. If you don't pray, say them to yourself, to your own racing mind, and let your breath slow. The bell holds the time.
Peace. The first word Jesus speaks to the storm: peace, be still. And the calm that leaves the disciples asking who he is. Today's word.

Your line: who is this. This week: sins first, the sabbath, the twelve, a widened family, the sower, the sleeping seed, the storm. Today, when something calms that you thought wouldn't, ask the disciples' question. Day two hundred three.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus did a weather miracle.
what it means: the disciples are left asking who can command the sea, a question the psalms answer.
what a scholar hears: pephimōso, be muzzled, the verb of the Capernaum exorcism; Psalm 106 [107] has God still the storm.
